Words | S. Li

Editors | Er Mu, Fanyu Meng

In the previous installment, Everything you wanted to know about noise-cancelling headphones, part 1, I introduced the non-adaptive feedforward ANC filter. This time, let’s talk about adaptive feedforward filters and see how ANC can adapt to your life!

As I mentioned at the end of the last article, the annoyingly fickle primary path (P(z)) and the person-specific secondary path (G(z)) make it hard for non-adaptive ANC filters to survive in academia… because the creed of academia is to drill into every crack and squeeze into every gap! For a feedforward filter, P(z) is the real nuisance; G(z) is comparatively tame. If we treat P(z) as a time-varying linear system, then by measuring the signals going into it and coming out of it, we can use an adaptive filter to track it and know its state at every moment. Okay, let’s set ANC aside for a moment and look at how a simple adaptive system-identification scheme works.

Figure 1. A non-adaptive system

To identify an unknown linear system A(z), the simplest method is to feed it an input test signal x(n), measure the output signal y(n), and take the ratio of output to input in the frequency domain: that ratio is the system.

Now let’s try a different approach. Forget that method; let’s see whether pure guesswork can do the job! As shown in Figure 1, we have an input signal x(n), the unknown system to be identified, A(z), and the output signal y(n). Let’s assume the system can be represented by an FIR filter of length N (that is, it has only zeros and no poles). Then A(z) can be represented in the time domain by a simple one-dimensional vector, 𝐚=[a0,a1,a2,...,aN−1] (the coefficients of the FIR filter). From here on, bold symbols denote vectors and non-bold symbols denote scalars. We call our guess the vector 𝐰 (in the frequency domain, this is W(z) in Figure 1). We take the signal going into the unknown system A(z), namely x(n), and feed it into W(z) as well; we invert the output (flip its phase by 180 degrees) and add it to the output of A(z), y(n), to get an error signal e(n). If this error signal is 0, we’ve guessed the system correctly! That is, 𝐚=𝐰.

So how do we guess the system? Put more plainly: how do we guess the numbers in 𝐰, all N of them? Doesn’t this feel just like guessing on a multiple-choice exam? Chinese students have their folklore for that: three short and one long, pick the long one; three long and one short, pick the short one; two long and two short, pick B… Anyway, let’s just guess one first. Er, wait, we have to guess N of them, and the range seems pretty wide. Oh well, let’s guess N zeros (𝐰=[0,0,0,...,0]) and see how lucky we get. Okay! Pens down! The teacher now checks your answers by testing the 𝐰 you handed in as shown in Figure 1: what is the error e(n)? I think we can all guess the result… e(n)=y(n)−0=y(n). Holding the results, the teacher says: “Look at you! What on earth have you done? You’re the worst student I’ve ever taught!”

Seeing the test results, you beg the teacher in tears: “Please give me one more chance!” Moved by your sincerity, the teacher says: “All right. Look at this test signal, x(n), then look at your test result, e(n), and think hard about how to find a better W(z)!”

After crossing a thousand mountains and rivers, you finally find, in the sacred text Adaptive Filter Theory [1], a simple but effective method: the method of steepest descent. Imagine you are on a mountaintop and want to get home at the foot of the mountain: find a path that leads downhill and just keep rolling down it.

https://gifimage.net/

Before handing in your next answer, your biggest worry is this: the last result was bad enough, so this one had better not be even worse. So first you define a cost function, called J(𝐰), and then head in the direction in which the cost function decreases! A commonly used cost function is the expected value of the squared error between the outputs of the system under test and the guessed system [1,2,3]:

J(𝐰)=𝐄{(y−𝐰*𝐱)2} (1)

One thing to note: in equation (1), * denotes convolution, which can also be expressed in vector form, for example as 𝐰𝐱T (many derivations use vectors, but the result is the same).

Now we need the gradient of this cost function, so that we can make it as small as possible. How? Take its partial derivative with respect to 𝐰 (for a parabola-like function, differentiation is the way to go):

∂J(𝐰)∂𝐰=−2𝐄{(y−𝐰*𝐱)𝐱} (2)

The new 𝐰 can then be calculated:

𝐰(2)=𝐰(1)−12μ∂J(𝐰)∂𝐰 (3)

Here 𝐰(1) is the first guess of the system coefficients and 𝐰(2) the second. A new symbol, μ, also appears: the step size, meaning how fast you walk down the mountain. Walk too fast and you’ll probably trip; walk too slowly and you’ll be late home for dinner. It looks simple, but it’s hard to carry out: what on earth do we do about that expectation?… Enter the name that pops up whenever you search Baidu or Google for ANC, optimization or machine learning: least mean squares (LMS, which has nothing to do with Siemens LMS, the test and simulation company). LMS says: “Stop overcomplicating things. Forget about expectations; just compute it at the current time step. Roll up your sleeves and get on with it!” Taking this advice, the answer to hand in this time is:

𝐰(2)=𝐰(1)−12μ(−2𝐱(1)𝐞(1))=𝐰(1)+μ𝐱(1)𝐞(1) (4)

x is also a one-dimensional vector of length N, the same length as 𝐰. At the current moment, say time k, it holds the most recent N samples: 𝐱(k)=[x(k),x(k−1),x(k−2),...x(k−N+1)]. Since this is only the second submission, the current time is obviously less than the length N, so the earlier samples are padded with zeros. You hand it in, the teacher checks it again and thinks: Well, well, not bad, better than last time! Looks like this kid has potential after all. I’ll give him back the results and see whether he can surprise me!

Back and forth, revising again and again, you finally work out the unknown system! You heave a long sigh: thank goodness for the teacher’s guidance! After all that rambling, this is what we call adaptation! The whole loop is shown in Figure 2. There are countless adaptive methods, and each one was proposed because earlier methods fell short in some application. That’s the academic habit of drilling into every crack I mentioned earlier.

Figure 2. System identification with an adaptive filter

Looking back, you gain a new insight into life: anyone you really want to get to know, you can come to know gradually by talking to them and getting feedback, until eventually you understand them. But one day they may drift away from you, and you may have to get to know a new friend. You don’t have to start from zero with the new person, though, because people always have something in common; you can bring all the experience you’ve built up to understanding them. In other words, this adaptive algorithm can also identify time-varying systems.

Now we can return to adaptive active noise cancellation. That fickle P(z)? We can tame it with an adaptive filter!

Figure 3. Simplified block diagram of adaptive feedforward ANC

Figure 3 shows a simplified block diagram of adaptive feedforward ANC. The ambient noise is recorded by the external Ref mic, filtered by the adaptive filter W(z), phase-inverted by 180 degrees and played through the headphone (which amounts to being filtered once more, by G(z)); the signal recorded by the internal Error mic is then fed back as the error. Unlike non-adaptive ANC, the adaptive filter can thus find a new, matching W(z) in real time.

At time k, the adaptive filter can be iterated as follows:

𝐰(k+1)=𝐰(k)+μ𝐱(k)𝐞(k) (5)

But compare Figures 2 and 3 and you’ll easily spot an extra G(z) in Figure 3. What does that mean? In the case of Figure 2, you hand your guess straight to the teacher, who tests your filter directly. With ANC headphones, though, you have to hand it to your group leader first, who passes it on to the teacher, and you correct your filter based on the teacher’s test results. That’s a bit worrying. What if your group leader is lazy and sits on your filter for a few days before handing it in (the delay of G(z)), or has some other bad habit, and so on… while all you can do is adjust your filter based on the test results the teacher gives you? To reduce this kind of trouble, the filtered-x LMS (FxLMS) method was born, as shown in Figure 4: before the adaptive algorithm is applied, the input signal is first filtered by a measured estimate, G′(z).

Figure 4. Simplified block diagram of filtered-x LMS adaptive feedforward ANC

The derivation is very simple: all the predicted output signals in equations 1–4 are filtered through G(z), so the predicted output becomes

y′=𝐰*𝐱*𝐠 (6)

So in the iteration, 𝐠 has to accompany every occurrence of x, where 𝐠 is the time-domain representation of G(z).

But as we all know, this G(z) exists physically: it is the transfer function from the headphone to the Error mic. All we can do is measure an estimate, 𝐠′, to stand in for it. At time k, the adaptive filter iteration can be modified to:

𝐰(k+1)=𝐰(k)+μ𝐱′(k)𝐞(k) (7)

𝐱′=𝐠′*𝐱(k) (8)

After all that chatter, this is the so-called FxLMS method. There are, of course, further refinements, such as normalized FxLMS, or FxNLMS, which replaces 𝐱′(k) in equation 7 with 𝐱′(k)|𝐱′(k)|2. The advantage is that the choice of step size μ becomes independent of the input signal and can be restricted to between 0 and 2 [1,2,3].

Another refinement is the psychoacoustics-based ANC mentioned in the previous article. At present, the sound pressure measured at the Error mic is used directly as the error measure. But in the end, whether noise cancellation is any good is something we hear, not data an instrument measures. When you shop for noise-cancelling headphones at the mall, have you ever seen a salesperson show you a noise-reduction curve on the spot? Everyone would rather put the headphones on and hear for themselves. In short, the proof of the pudding is in the eating: just put them on and listen.

So, as shown in Figure 5, some researchers apply a weighting filter to the error to estimate how loud we actually perceive it, for example an A-weighting filter [4]. Correspondingly, the signal must also be weighted before it enters the adaptive algorithm, for the same reason as with G(z). So now, on top of the group leader, there’s a class monitor too!

Figure 5. Simplified block diagram of psychoacoustics-based adaptive feedforward ANC

These algorithms look great, but reality bites. When we read academic papers, we tend to be dazzled by their godlike algorithms and elegant conclusions and overlook the premise behind each method: “under condition xxx.” Naturally, the adaptive feedforward filter comes with prerequisites too. To pick out the most important one: the signals picked up by the Ref mic and the Error mic must be highly correlated. Don’t laugh, and don’t assume these two signals couldn’t possibly be uncorrelated. Not so fast; anything is possible. Here’s a real-life example: a mischievous user wearing noise-cancelling headphones grabs them and rubs them up, down, left and right against their ears. Er… and no, this is not the “rubbing, rubbing” of skateboard shoes on a shiny floor from the Chinese meme song “My Skateboard Shoes”… The sound this rubbing makes is hard for the Ref mic to pick up, but the Error mic records a very loud sound.

You handed in a perfectly good filter and still got a dressing-down from the teacher. Upset, you start tweaking the coefficients at random, and if you’re not careful, forget noise cancellation: you might end up with noise amplification instead.

At this point, some of you might object: but company xx clearly uses LMS in its headphones! And plenty of papers on headphone ANC say in their introductions that LMS is a method commonly used in noise-cancelling headphones…… er……

That’s because LMS doesn’t have to be applied in real time like this. It can also be applied offline:

Remember the method for calculating the feedforward filter from the last article? Play a test sound from an external loudspeaker, record it with the Ref mic and the Error mic, obtain two transfer functions, use them to calculate P(z) for one fixed direction, and then use that P(z) to calculate the feedforward filter.

Well, I can also obtain P(z) with LMS. Same setup: play white noise from an external loudspeaker (any broadband signal will do, but make it a bit longer) and record it with the Ref mic and the Error mic. Now I have the input signal and the sound pressure recorded without noise cancellation, corresponding to x(n) and y(n) in Figures 3 to 5. Okay, now I can run a simulation on the computer: use LMS to compute the noise-cancelling filter from x(n) and y(n), giving W(z), and then load the resulting filter coefficients into the headphones.

So this method is basically the same as the non-adaptive method in the last article: it computes the filter for one particular direction. But would you call it an LMS method? At best, it’s an offline adaptive method. There are indeed a few genuinely real-time adaptive noise-cancelling headphones on the market, but as far as I know they are very, very few, and computing adaptive filters in real time comes with many limitations and is reserved for special scenarios. I’d love to know which noise-cancelling headphones on the market really adapt in real time, so please tell me!

One more thing about the fickle G(z): measuring G(z) in real time across all kinds of situations (headphones worn sideways, upright, at a tilt) is pretty hard, and everyone is still working on it. But measuring each person’s G(z) is feasible. Some headphones have a personalization feature: after you put them on, they tell you a test sound is about to play, and that test sound can be used to measure G(z). As for measuring it moment by moment, that’s a hot research topic. As I said, academia drills into every crack. But whether it can make it into products, er……

That’s about it for the basics of feedforward filters. Their drawbacks are fairly obvious: noise cancellation relies mainly on the input signal measured by the Ref mic as the main source of noise. That raises some doubts. Does the noise always come from outside? Can the Ref mic always pick it up? And with a non-adaptive filter, the noise reduction depends on direction. These doubts gave rise to the feedback noise-cancelling filter. In the next installment, I’ll go over the general design approach for feedback filters.

Author: S. Li

An acoustics PhD student who has spent years drifting around Germany, working mainly on binaural audio, psychoacoustics and active noise cancellation.
